Use it to create realistic testing environments with complex evaluation criteria, that can be shared as simple files and tested in production warehouses, while making it as easy as possible to create new tasks.
It does this by running each task in a separate temporary sandbox, and then evaluating the agent's work against the expected results.
If all of them pass, the task passes. If any fail, the task fails.

ADE Bench evaluates analytics and data engineering tasks using real dbt projects and databases.
Mean tokens is the average number of assistant-generated tokens across all valid rollouts, including successful and unsuccessful attempts.
Rollouts interrupted by infrastructure issues are excluded.
DeepSWE 1.1 uses mini-swe-agent, while the other three benchmarks use Terminus 2.
All four use a 512k-token limit, temperature 1, top_p 0.95, and max reasoning.
Each model generated 16 rollouts per task.
Reasoning tokens account for roughly 90% of the token savings on Terminal-Bench 2.1, ReactBench, and ADE.
Across these benchmarks, Particle-1 uses 28.4%–52.2% fewer output tokens and achieves 34.4%–51.6% lower average cost per task
Both models implemented the same three staging-layer casts, but Particle-1 used 1,757 tokens for the edit call compared with 3,485 for the base model.

Particle-1 reused the existing surrogate-key macro, while the base model implemented an incrementing key with additional bookkeeping and incremental validation; the main edit call used 1,602 versus 8,722 output tokens
Pass@1 rates are within the confidence intervals of the base model.
